## New Cross-Domain Connection

- **[2026-10-28] The wiki has three pages on bet sizing, and all three size one bet at a time. Fred's two live books both run many bets at once. The rewritten Carlisle page is the first source in the wiki to name that gap, and it gives a holding-count rule the paper book's ">35 rule" has never had a reason for.** [[finance/concepts/concept-kelly-criterion]] and [[finance/michael-burry/burry-vs-kelly-sizing]] both treat Kelly as a per-opportunity fraction. [[sports-betting/bankroll-management]] plans "fractional Kelly (e.g. 25%)" per bet. None of them mentions concurrent or correlated bets. In [[podcasts/podcast-behind-the-balance-sheet-tobias-carlisle]] (now rewritten from the transcript), Carlisle says he is sceptical of applying Kelly literally when many positive-expectation bets run at once. His alternative is a ruin-avoidance holding count: about 30 positions for most portfolios and about 100 in small and micro caps. [[finance/paper-trading/paper-trading-portfolio]] runs about 35 flat $1,000 positions at once, with a ">35 rule" that forces capacity trims (NOC and OXY on 09-28/29, MCK on 10-27). That ceiling comes from the €30k capital cap, not from any ruin logic. The book also holds Strategies F (small-cap value) and G (small-cap growth) at the same $1,000 size as large caps, which is the bucket where Carlisle would want roughly three times the breadth. A weekend football slate raises the same issue for Sports Betting: several Kelly-sized stakes settle together, so per-bet Kelly adds up to more than the bankroll can stand. The concrete gap is a "simultaneous bets" section in the Kelly concept page. It would cover the known result that summed per-bet Kelly over-commits when bets run in parallel, and *Fortune's Formula* (already on [[books/books-from-podcasts]]) as the book-length source. Both the 35 cap and the bankroll stub could then cite it.

## Books from podcasts (3 new)

- *Buffett: The Making of an American Capitalist* (Roger Lowenstein), Gracián's aphorisms (probably *The Art of Worldly Wisdom*), *Quantitative Value* (Tobias Carlisle): all from the rewritten BTBS Tobias Carlisle episode page.

## New Cross-Domain Connection

- **[2026-10-27] The paper-trader bought Leidos on 10-26 as a name with "no AI-capex… overlap". But Burry's Palantir short thesis, which Fred holds a live put on, says Palantir is the same kind of business as Leidos: engineers deployed on site to wire software into government systems. Together with the live Accenture long, the book is making a relative-value bet that integrators' multiples will converge, and nothing in it says so.** [[finance/paper-trading/trades/2026-10-26-LDOS]] thesis point 4 calls LDOS a diversifier because it isn't on Burry's short list (which includes PLTR). [[finance/short-research/source-burry-palantir-new-clothes-2026-02-12]] argues Palantir is "fundamentally a consultancy". On his reading, its Forward-Deployed Engineers integrate clients' existing SAP/Oracle/Accenture systems for months at a time, and the company is priced like SaaS only because that labour is booked outside cost of goods sold. [[ai-tech/source-palantir-nvidia-nemotron-2026-07-02]] gives the bull version: Palantir as the government's model-agnostic "trusted intermediary" for AI. That is the role a defence IT integrator like Leidos sells, and DoD units are already routing Nemotron work through Palantir. [[finance/trading-portfolio]] holds the PLTR put (≈€310) next to ACN (+57%, the commercial version of the same model). So LDOS and PLTR sit on opposite sides of one question: does government AI spending go to the integrator priced at 11x guidance or to the one priced as software? The put and LDOS/ACN pay off in the same scenario, a re-rating of Palantir toward a consultancy multiple. In the other scenario, where Palantir takes share, both lose. One more risk applies to LDOS and ACN but not to PLTR: AI deflation of billable hours. [[technology/source-salesforce-agentic-engineering-2026]] reports a migration estimated at 231 person-days finished in 13 days with Claude Code. That is the billable-hours base of a services integrator, and the AI-risk table's bubble-only test (09-29 connection) misses it again here. **Check at LDOS's Q3 (~Nov 3) and ACN's next print:** look for any mention of Palantir as a competitor or partner, and whether fixed-price or AI-delivered work is compressing headcount-linked revenue.

No new investigation ideas; no older items resolved; no new podcast books.
